title: Homework
resolution: Resolved: Elementary schools should eliminate graded homework.
summary: Research links homework to achievement much more strongly in the upper grades than in elementary school. Should elementary schools stop assigning graded homework?

background.p: A review of more than 60 studies led by Duke psychologist Harris Cooper (2006) found that homework has a positive link to achievement, and that the link is stronger in grades 7–12 than in elementary school. Many teachers follow a "10-minute rule": about ten minutes a night per grade level, so about 40 minutes in fourth grade. Cooper also found that very large amounts were not linked to higher achievement, even in high school.

For younger students, Cooper suggested homework may mainly build study habits and time management rather than raise grades, and recommended short assignments that students can complete successfully. A 2014 Stanford study of students at ten high-performing high schools (Pope and colleagues) found they averaged about three hours of homework a night and many named it as a main source of stress. That study was of high schoolers, not elementary students.

disputed.q: Does homework help elementary students learn?
positions: Reviews find only a small link between homework and achievement in elementary grades.
Supporters reply that small amounts of practice and the habits it builds pay off later, and that the research measures mostly test scores, not habits.

terms.def: Work done at home that counts toward a student's grade. The resolution covers graded homework only; optional practice and reading at home could continue.
The idea that spaced, repeated practice helps learning last.
A common guideline of about ten minutes of homework per night per grade level.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: In elementary school, graded homework costs family time and causes stress without clear learning gains.

args.claim: Graded homework does little for young students' achievement.
args.warrant: If a policy takes time every night, it should have clear benefits. Reviews find the homework-achievement link is weak in the elementary grades, so the time costs more than it returns.
args.evidence: Cooper's 2006 review (Duke) finding a stronger link in grades 7–12 than in elementary school; later reviews of the homework literature.
args.response: The negative replies that a weak link in test scores doesn't measure the habits homework builds, which the same researcher stresses.

args.claim: Grading homework measures home help, not learning.
args.warrant: Some children have a parent who can help every night; others have parents working evenings or who don't speak English. Grading the result rewards the home, not the child.
args.evidence: Research on homework and family resources; teacher surveys on unequal home support.
args.response: The negative argues that teachers can design homework children can do alone, and grading it lightly keeps students accountable.

args.claim: Evenings are better used for reading, play, sleep and family.
args.warrant: Young children learn through free reading, conversation and play, and they need sleep; time on worksheets crowds these out.
args.evidence: Pediatric guidance on sleep and play; research on reading for pleasure and vocabulary growth.
args.response: The negative replies that ten or twenty minutes is a small part of an evening, and many families value the routine.

args.warrant: Teachers can still send home optional practice and reading logs. Removing grades ends the penalty for children whose homes can't support homework, without ending learning at home.
args.evidence: Districts that have adopted no-graded-homework or reading-only policies, and their reports.
args.response: The negative argues that optional work is often skipped by the students who need practice most, as studies of ungraded practice have found.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Short, purposeful homework builds skills and habits that pay off for years.

args.warrant: Spelling, math facts and reading fluency improve with spaced practice; school hours alone may not give enough repetitions.
args.evidence: Cognitive science research on spaced practice and retrieval; Cooper's finding of a positive (if smaller) link in younger grades.
args.response: The affirmative answers that practice can happen in school or at home without being graded, so the resolution doesn't stop it.

args.claim: Homework builds study habits before the stakes rise.
args.warrant: Students who learn to manage small assignments in elementary school are ready for heavier loads in middle and high school, where homework matters more.
args.evidence: Cooper's observation that elementary homework may mainly build time management and study skills; teacher reports on the middle-school transition.
args.response: The affirmative replies that habits can be taught through school routines and optional work; grades aren't what build them.

args.claim: Grades keep homework meaningful and fair.
args.warrant: When homework doesn't count, many students skip it, often those who need practice most, and teachers lose a picture of who needs help.
args.evidence: Research on ungraded practice (for example, Huey et al., 2022, summarized by the University of Rochester, finding completion fell when homework didn't count); teacher surveys.
args.response: The affirmative argues that the same research found some gains when homework was removed from grades, and teachers can check work without grading it.

args.claim: Homework connects parents to what children are learning.
args.warrant: Seeing assignments lets parents follow progress and spot problems early.
args.evidence: Studies of parent involvement in school; Cooper's recommendation that some elementary homework involve parents.
args.response: The affirmative answers that newsletters, conferences and ungraded work do this without the stress of grades.

strawmen.strawman: They think kids should never have to work hard.
strawmen.why: Supporters of the resolution object to graded homework for young children, not to effort or practice.
strawmen.steelman: Research finds little achievement benefit from elementary homework, and grading it rewards home support more than learning, so practice should be optional and evenings left for reading, play and sleep.

strawmen.strawman: They just want to keep kids busy every night.
strawmen.why: Defenders of homework point to practice effects and study habits, and most support small amounts.
strawmen.steelman: Short, purposeful homework gives practice that helps skills last and builds habits students need later; grading keeps it meaningful.

weak.why: Research finds a positive link in the upper grades and small benefits in younger ones; calling it pointless is easy to refute.

weak.arg: If we don't grade homework, kids will stop learning.
weak.why: Students learn mostly in class; this exaggerates what homework does.

aff: Would your plan still allow optional practice?
How would teachers know who needs extra help?
Does the research measure study habits, or only test scores?
neg: How many minutes a night do you think is right for a second grader?
What should happen to a student whose parents can't help?
Would ungraded practice give the same benefits?
